## Appendix B The $T$ -matrix from Lippmann-Schwinger equation

Starting with the Lippmann-Schwinger equation for the in/out-states in terms of the free-particle basis states, either (3.2) or equivalently

$$ \displaystyle|\alpha\rangle^{\mathrm{in/out}} \displaystyle=\Big(1+\frac{1}{E_{\alpha}-\widehat{\mathcal{H}}\pm i\epsilon}\widehat{V}\Big)|\alpha\rangle^{0}, $$

we can rewrite the S-matrix elements as

$$ \displaystyle{}^{\mathrm{out}}\langle\beta|\alpha\rangle^{\mathrm{in}} \displaystyle={}^{0}\langle\beta|{\alpha}\rangle^{\rm in}+{}^{0}\langle{\beta}|\widehat{V}\frac{1}{E_{\beta}-\widehat{\mathcal{H}}+i\epsilon}|\alpha\rangle^{\rm in} \displaystyle=\,^{0}\langle\beta|\alpha\rangle^{0}+\,^{0}\langle\beta|\frac{1}{E_{\alpha}-\widehat{\mathcal{H}}_{2}+i\epsilon}\widehat{V}|\alpha\rangle^{\mathrm{in}}+\frac{1}{E_{\beta}-E_{\alpha}+i\epsilon}\,^{0}\langle\beta|\widehat{V}|\alpha\rangle^{\mathrm{in}} \displaystyle=\,^{0}\langle\beta|\alpha\rangle^{0}-2\pi i\delta(E_{\alpha}-E_{\beta})\,{}^{0}\langle\beta|\widehat{V}|\alpha\rangle^{\textrm{in}}, $$

where we used (B.1) for ${}^{\rm out}\langle{\beta}|$ in the first equality, and (3.2) for $|{\alpha}\rangle^{\rm in}$ in the second equality. This gives (3.3) with the expression (3.4) for the $T$ -matrix element.

## Appendix C Glossary of notations

In this Appendix we recap various symbols introduced in this paper, and list some additional useful relations.

In the $2\to 2$ scattering process, we label the incoming momenta by $p_{1},p_{2}$ , and the outgoing momenta by $p_{3},p_{4}$ . The gauge-singlet particle/anti-particle in-state $|\vec{p}_{1},\vec{p}_{2}\rangle^{\rm in}$ is normalized covariantly according to ${}^{\rm in}\langle\vec{p}_{3},\vec{p}_{4}|\vec{p}_{1},\vec{p}_{2}\rangle^{\rm in}=I(p_{3},p_{4}|p_{1},p_{2})$ (1.3), and similarly for the out-state $|\vec{p}_{3},\vec{p}_{4}\rangle^{\rm out}$ .

In lightcone coordinates, the mass-shell relation reads $-p_{i}^{-}={(p_{i}^{\perp})^{2}+m^{2}\over 2p_{i}^{+}}$ . Working at fixed total lightcone momentum $P^{+}=p_{1}^{+}+p_{2}^{+}=p_{3}^{+}+p_{4}^{+}$ , we parameterize the incoming momenta with $(x,p)$ , and the outgoing momentum by $(y,q)$ , defined in (1.6). Further working at a fixed Mandelstam variables $s=-(p_{1}+p_{2})^{2}=-(p_{3}+p_{4})^{2}$ , we have labeled the in-states with $(x,a=\pm)$ , and the out-states with $(y,b=\pm)$ . The transverse momenta $p$ and $q$ are related by

$$ \displaystyle p=a\,\ell_{*}(x),~~~~q=b\,\ell_{*}(y), $$

with $\ell_{*}$ defined in (3.23).

The asymptotic states in the lightfront quantization are deonted $|x,p\rangle^{\rm in}$ and $|y,q\rangle^{\rm out}$ respectively. They are related to the covariant basis states by a normalization factor ${\cal N}({\alpha})$ , as in (3.29) and (3.30). The phase of ${\cal N}({\alpha})$ , denoted $e^{i\varphi({\alpha})}$ , is determined through (4.28), (4.30), and (4.6). In other words, we found $\varphi({\alpha})=(1+\widetilde{\lambda})\varphi^{(0)}({\alpha})$ , where $\varphi^{(0)}({\alpha})$ is the tree-level phase correction (4.6).

Alternatively, we can label the in- and out-states in the center-of-mass frame by the angles ${\alpha}$ and ${\beta}$ , defined in (3.27). They are related to $(x,p)$ and $(y,q)$ by

$$ \displaystyle \displaystyle\cos\alpha={\sqrt{s}\over\sqrt{s-4m^{2}}}(1-2x),~~~~{\rm sign}(\sin\alpha)=-{\rm sign}(p), \displaystyle\cos{\beta}={\sqrt{s}\over\sqrt{s-4m^{2}}}(1-2y),~~~~{\rm sign}(\sin{\beta})=-{\rm sign}(q). $$

The scattering angle $\theta\equiv{\beta}-{\alpha}$ can be expressed in terms of $(x,a)$ and $(y,b)$ through

$$ \displaystyle\cot{\theta\over 2} \displaystyle={1\over\sqrt{s}}\left[-2im+i{x(1-x)y(1-y)\over(x-y)(s-4m^{2})}u_{a}^{-}(x)u_{b}^{+}(y)(u_{a}^{+}(x)-u_{b}^{-}(y))\right], $$

where $u_{a}^{\pm}(x)$ are defined in (4.7).

The part of the lightcone Hamiltonian relevant for the planar singlet channel amplitude is (2.19). The interaction $\widehat{\mathcal{H}}_{4}^{\rm S}$ is expanded in terms of the fermion creation and annihilation operators with coefficient $\mathcal{H}_{4}^{\rm reg}$ defined in (2.21). The latter is further separated (2.22) into a classical term $\mathcal{H}_{4}^{\rm cl}$ (2.23) and a counter term ${\cal C}_{4}$ (2.24). The interaction “potential” ${\mathcal{V}}^{ba}(y|x)$ appearing in the manifestly finite integral equation (3.25) is none other than a rewriting of $\mathcal{H}_{4}^{\rm cl}$ (3.26) in terms of the variables $(x,a)$ and $(y,b)$ at fixed $s$ .

The $2\to 2$ scattering amplitude in the singlet channel is expressed through the $T$ -matrix. The covariant $T$ -matrix element $T_{\rm S}(s,\theta)$ is defined in (1.2), and is decomposed in terms of the forward-distribution coefficient $T_{0}(s)$ , and the function part $\widetilde{T}(s,\theta)$ , defined in (1.4). The analogous $T$ -matrix elements in the lightfront basis is denoted $\mathcal{T}(y,q|x,p)$ or equivalently at fixed $s$ , $\mathcal{T}^{ba}(y|x)$ , and decomposed into the forward-distribution coefficient $\mathcal{T}_{0}(x)$ and the function part $\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}^{ba}(y|x)$ via (1.8). Their relation to the covariant $T$ -matrix element is given in (1.10). The $T$ -matrix element at $L$ -loop order is denoted, after stripped off the factor $\lambda^{L+1}$ , by the same symbol with a superscript $(L)$ .

## Appendix D Derivation of the finite integral equation

We begin with the observation that $\delta_{C}(q,y|p,x;\delta,\Lambda)$ defined in (3.18) vanishes in the $\delta\to 0$ limit, and is regular at $x=0,1$ . Consider the $L$ -loop amplitude ( $L>1$ )

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{T}^{(L)}(y,q|x,p) \displaystyle=\lim_{\Lambda\to\infty}\lim_{\delta\to 0}{(P^{+})^{2}\over(2\pi)^{2}}\mathchoice{{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle-$}}\kern-4.86108pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}}\kern-3.43057pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}}\kern-2.908pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}}\kern-2.76045pt}}\!\int_{\frac{\delta}{P^{+}}}^{1-\frac{\delta}{P^{+}}}dz\int_{-\Lambda}^{\Lambda}d\ell\,G(z,\ell|x,p;\varepsilon) \displaystyle\times\Bigg[\mathcal{T}^{(0)}(y,q|z,\ell)\mathcal{T}^{(L-1)}(z,\ell|x,p)+\lambda^{-2}\mathcal{C}_{4}(y,q|z.\ell;\delta,\Lambda)\mathcal{T}^{(L-2)}(z,\ell|x,p)\Bigg], $$

where

$$ G(z,\ell|x,p;\epsilon)=\bigg[\frac{p^{2}+m^{2}}{2x(1-x)}-\frac{\ell^{2}+m^{2}}{2z(1-z)}+i\epsilon\bigg]^{-1}. $$

Using (3.18), we can write

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{T}^{(L)}(y,q|x,p) \displaystyle=\lim_{\Lambda\to\infty}\lim_{\delta\to 0}{(P^{+})^{2}\over(2\pi)^{2}}\mathchoice{{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle-$}}\kern-4.86108pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}}\kern-3.43057pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}}\kern-2.908pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}}\kern-2.76045pt}}\!\int_{\frac{\delta}{P^{+}}}^{1-\frac{\delta}{P^{+}}}dz\int_{-\Lambda}^{\Lambda}d\ell\,G(z,\ell|x,p;\epsilon)\Bigg[\mathcal{T}^{(0}(y,q|z,\ell)\mathcal{T}^{(L-1)}(z,\ell|x,p) \displaystyle+{\Lambda(P^{+})^{2}\over 2\pi^{2}}\mathchoice{{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle-$}}\kern-4.86108pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}}\kern-3.43057pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}}\kern-2.908pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}}\kern-2.76045pt}}\!\int_{\frac{\delta}{P^{+}}}^{1-\frac{\delta}{P^{+}}}dz^{\prime}\,\,{2z^{\prime}(1-z^{\prime})\overline{\mathcal{T}}^{(0)}_{\infty}(y|z^{\prime})\mathcal{T}^{(0)}_{\infty}(z^{\prime}|z)}\,\mathcal{T}^{(L-2)}(z,\ell|x,p) \displaystyle+\lambda^{-2}\delta_{C}(y,q|z,\ell;\delta,\Lambda)\mathcal{T}^{(L-2)}(z,\ell|x,p)\Bigg]. $$

Assuming that $\mathcal{T}$ has at most a simple pole at $z=0,1$ , which will be justified a posteriori, together with the facts that $K$ vanishes at $z=0,1$ and that $\delta_{C}$ is regular in the integration range, we conclude that the last term in the bracket of (D.3) has a vanishing contribution. Next, we change the order of integration in the second line of (D.3) and write

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{T}^{(L)}(y,q|x,p)=\lim_{\Lambda\to\infty}\lim_{\delta\to 0}\Bigg[{(P^{+})^{2}\over(2\pi)^{2}}\mathchoice{{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle-$}}\kern-4.86108pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}}\kern-3.43057pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}}\kern-2.908pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}}\kern-2.76045pt}}\!\int_{\frac{\delta}{P^{+}}}^{1-\frac{\delta}{P^{+}}}dz\int_{-\Lambda}^{\Lambda}d\ell\,G(z,\ell|x,p;\epsilon)\mathcal{T}^{(0)}(y,q|z,\ell)\mathcal{T}^{(L-1)}(z,\ell|x,p) \displaystyle+{\Lambda(P^{+})^{4}\over 8\pi^{4}}\,\mathchoice{{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle-$}}\kern-4.86108pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}}\kern-3.43057pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}}\kern-2.908pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}}\kern-2.76045pt}}\!\int_{\frac{\delta}{P^{+}}}^{1-\frac{\delta}{P^{+}}}dz^{\prime}\,\,2z^{\prime}(1-z^{\prime})\overline{\mathcal{T}}^{(0)}_{\infty}(y|z^{\prime})\mathchoice{{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle-$}}\kern-4.86108pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}}\kern-3.43057pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}}\kern-2.908pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}}\kern-2.76045pt}}\!\int_{\frac{\delta}{P^{+}}}^{1-\frac{\delta}{P^{+}}}dz\int_{-\Lambda}^{\Lambda}d\ell\,G(z,\ell|x,p;\epsilon)\mathcal{T}^{(0)}_{\infty}(z^{\prime}|z)\mathcal{T}^{(L-2)}(z,\ell|x,p)\Bigg]. $$

In the second line, the $z^{\prime}$ -integral can at most produce a log divergence in $\delta$ , while the $z$ -integral gives a non-singular power series in $\delta$ . Furthermore, the $\ell$ -integral gives a result that is finite in the $\Lambda\to\infty$ limit. Therefore, we can take the limit on the $z,\ell$ integral, giving

$$ \displaystyle \displaystyle\mathcal{T}^{(L)}(y,q|x,p)=\lim_{\Lambda\to\infty}\lim_{\delta\to 0}\Bigg[{(P^{+})^{2}\over(2\pi)^{2}}\mathchoice{{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle-$}}\kern-4.86108pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}}\kern-3.43057pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}}\kern-2.908pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}}\kern-2.76045pt}}\!\int_{\frac{\delta}{P^{+}}}^{1-\frac{\delta}{P^{+}}}dz\int_{-\Lambda}^{\Lambda}d\ell\,G(z,\ell|x,p;\epsilon)\mathcal{T}^{(0)}(y,q|z,\ell)\mathcal{T}^{(L-1)}(z,\ell|x,p) \displaystyle+{\Lambda(P^{+})^{4}\over 8\pi^{4}}\mathchoice{{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle-$}}\kern-4.86108pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}}\kern-3.43057pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}}\kern-2.908pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}}\kern-2.76045pt}}\!\int_{\frac{\delta}{P^{+}}}^{1-\frac{\delta}{P^{+}}}dz^{\prime}\,2z^{\prime}(1-z^{\prime})\overline{\mathcal{T}}^{(0)}_{\infty}(y|z^{\prime})\mathchoice{{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle-$}}\kern-4.86108pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}}\kern-3.43057pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}}\kern-2.908pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}}\kern-2.76045pt}}\!\int_{0}^{1}dz\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\ell\,G(\ell,z|x,p;\epsilon)\mathcal{T}^{(0)}_{\infty}(z^{\prime}|z)\mathcal{T}^{(n-2)}(z,\ell|x,p)\Bigg]. $$

Next, we reintroduce a trivial $\ell^{\prime}$ -integral, and then relabel $z^{\prime},\ell^{\prime}\leftrightarrow z,\ell$ ,

$$ \displaystyle \displaystyle\mathcal{T}^{(L)}(y,q|x,p)=\lim_{\Lambda\to\infty}\lim_{\delta\to 0}{(P^{+})^{2}\over(2\pi)^{2}}\mathchoice{{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle-$}}\kern-4.86108pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}}\kern-3.43057pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}}\kern-2.908pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}}\kern-2.76045pt}}\!\int_{\frac{\delta}{P^{+}}}^{1-\frac{\delta}{P^{+}}}dz\int_{-\Lambda}^{\Lambda}d\ell\,G(z,\ell|x,p;\epsilon)\Bigg[\mathcal{T}^{(0)}(y,q|z,\ell)\mathcal{T}^{(L-1)}(z,\ell|x,p) \displaystyle+{(P^{+})^{2}\over 2\pi^{2}}z(1-z)\overline{\mathcal{T}}^{(0)}_{\infty}(y|z)\mathchoice{{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle-$}}\kern-4.86108pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}}\kern-3.43057pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}}\kern-2.908pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}}\kern-2.76045pt}}\!\int_{0}^{1}dz^{\prime}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\ell^{\prime}\,G(z^{\prime},\ell^{\prime}|x,p;\epsilon)\,\mathcal{T}^{(0)}_{\infty}(z|z^{\prime})\mathcal{T}^{(L-2)}(z^{\prime},\ell^{\prime}|x,p)\Bigg]. $$

By inspecting (3.14) and the definition (3.22), we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{\infty}(z|x,p) \displaystyle=\lim_{\Lambda\to\infty}\lim_{\delta\to 0}\Bigg[\lambda\mathcal{T}^{(0)}_{\infty}(z|x)+\lambda{(P^{+})^{2}\over(2\pi)^{2}}\mathchoice{{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle-$}}\kern-4.86108pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle-$}}\kern-3.43057pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}}\kern-2.908pt}}{{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle-$}}\kern-2.76045pt}}\!\int_{\frac{\delta}{P^{+}}}^{1-\frac{\delta}{P^{+}}}dz^{\prime}\int_{-\Lambda}^{\Lambda}d\ell^{\prime}\,G(\ell^{\prime},z^{\prime};\varepsilon)\mathcal{T}^{(0)}_{\infty}(z|z^{\prime})\mathcal{T}(z^{\prime},\ell^{\prime}|x,p)\Bigg], $$

We see that (D.5) is precisely $L$ -loop (i.e. order $\lambda^{L+1}$ ) part of (3.21), for $L>1$ .

## Appendix E Numerical check of the all-order solution

In this appendix, we verify numerically that the analytic ansatz (4.31), together with the coupling redefinition (1.11), satisfies the integral equation (4.22). This is performed by a direct comparison of the two sides of (4.22) evaluated with the ansatz.

*Figure 8: Numerical tests of the integral equation at coupling $\tilde{\lambda}=1/4$ and scattering angle $\theta=\beta-\alpha=\pi/4$ for a range of $s$ (having set $m=1$ ). The left panel compares the real part of $\widetilde{T}(s,\theta)$ (black) to $\sum_{L=0}^{n}\lambda^{L+1}\widetilde{T}^{(L)}(s,\theta)$ (orange) up to three-loop order. The right panel compares the imaginary part, with all-order results in black, and perturbative results in purple. The deviation between the two sides of the integral equation for the all-orders ansatz is shown in the lower panels.*

Figure 8 shows such a numerical test for the real and imaginary part of the function part of the amplitude in the covariant basis, $\widetilde{T}(s,\theta)$ , at $\widetilde{\lambda}={1\over 4}$ and scattering angle $\theta={\pi\over 4}$ over a range of $s$ . As Lorentz invariance is not manifest in (4.22), we have chosen the incoming angle ${\alpha}={\pi\over 2}$ and outgoing angle ${\beta}={3\pi\over 4}$ . The numerical integral is evaluated using the “PrincipalValue” method of NIntegrate in Mathematica. The agreement with the integral equation is well within 7 significant digits. We have also included a comparison with the perturbative results up to $n$ -loop ordfer, for $n=1,2,3$ . The perturbative convergence supports the claim of a unique solution to (3.25).
